title: Hreflang return links: audit them with a short Python script and no dependencies
summary:
Hreflang fails quietly. When two language pages do not point at each other, Google does not show an error in your browser or in the page. The annotation simply does not do its job, and the first sign is the wrong language version ranking in the wrong country.

This tutorial builds a small checker that fetches one page, follows the alternates it lists, and reports missing return links, missing self-references, malformed codes and relative URLs. It uses only the Python standard library.

What the rules actually say

Everything below comes from Google's page on localized versions. I read it in full before writing the code.

  • Every version must list itself and all other versions, including the default page.
  • Alternate URLs must be fully qualified, with the protocol. A root-relative path like /de/ is not enough.
  • Links must be reciprocal. If page X points to page Y, page Y must point back to X, otherwise Google may ignore or misread the annotations.
  • x-default is for a language selector or a fallback for unmatched languages.
  • The language part is ISO 639-1 and the optional region part is ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2. A country code on its own is not valid, because the first code must be a language.
  • Reserved region codes such as EU, UN and UK are ignored. This catches the common en-UK, where the correct region for the United Kingdom is GB.
  • HTML tags, an HTTP Link header and an XML sitemap are treated as equivalent. Pick one.

This script checks the HTML method only. If your site uses sitemap annotations, the same logic applies, but you would parse xhtml:link entries instead.

Step 1: read the annotations from the head

Hreflang tags belong in the . The parser below collects rel="alternate" links that carry an hreflang attribute, and stops reading once the starts, so a stray link in the body is not counted.

class HreflangParser(HTMLParser):
    """Collect "alternate" hreflang=...> from the  only."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.entries = []
        self._in_head = False
        self._done = False

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if self._done:
            return
        if tag == "head":
            self._in_head = True
        elif tag == "body":
            self._done = True
        elif tag == "link" and self._in_head:
            a = {k.lower(): (v or "") for k, v in attrs}
            rels = a.get("rel", "").lower().split()
            if "alternate" in rels and a.get("hreflang"):
                self.entries.append((a["hreflang"].strip(), a.get("href", "").strip()))

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag == "head":
            self._done = True

Splitting rel on whitespace matters, because rel="alternate home" is valid HTML. Lowercasing attribute names handles HREFLANG= written in uppercase.

Step 2: check each code 

RESERVED_REGIONS = {"EU", "UN", "UK"}
CODE_RE = re.compile(r"^([a-zA-Z]{2})(?:-([a-zA-Z]{4}))?(?:-([a-zA-Z]{2}))?$")


def check_code(code):
    """Return a list of problems with one hreflang value (empty if fine)."""
    if code.lower() == "x-default":
        return []
    m = CODE_RE.match(code)
    if not m:
        return [f"malformed code '{code}'"]
    region = m.group(3)
    if region and region.upper() in RESERVED_REGIONS:
        return [f"reserved region '{region.upper()}' in '{code}' is ignored by Google"]
    return []

The pattern accepts a two-letter language, an optional four-letter script and an optional two-letter region. That catches en_GB (underscore) and english. It does not catch a country code used on its own. A bare us is two letters, so it passes the shape check even though Google needs a language first. The script does not carry the full ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1 lists, so it cannot tell a real language from an unused two-letter pair. Add those lists if you need that guarantee.

Step 3: audit the return links

This is the core. It compares every page against every alternate it lists.

def audit(pages):
    """pages: {url: [(hreflang, href), ...]}. Returns a list of issue dicts."""
    issues = []
    lookup = {norm(u): {norm(h) for _, h in e if h} for u, e in pages.items()}
    # targets listed with a real language code, excluding x-default entries
    lang_lookup = {
        norm(u): {norm(h) for c, h in e if h and c.lower() != "x-default"}
        for u, e in pages.items()
    }

    for url, entries in pages.items():
        if not entries:
            issues.append({"url": url, "level": "info", "msg": "no hreflang annotations"})
            continue
        codes = [c.lower() for c, _ in entries]
        for code, href in entries:
            for problem in check_code(code):
                issues.append({"url": url, "level": "error", "msg": problem})
            if not re.match(r"^https?://", href):
                issues.append({"url": url, "level": "error",
                               "msg": f"'{code}' href is not fully qualified: '{href}'"})
        for c in sorted({c for c in codes if codes.count(c) > 1}):
            issues.append({"url": url, "level": "error", "msg": f"duplicate hreflang '{c}'"})
        if norm(url) not in {norm(h) for _, h in entries}:
            issues.append({"url": url, "level": "error", "msg": "page does not list itself"})
        if "x-default" not in codes:
            issues.append({"url": url, "level": "warning", "msg": "no x-default entry"})
        for code, href in entries:
            target = norm(href)
            if target == norm(url) or target not in lookup:
                continue  # self, or a page we did not audit
            if norm(url) not in lookup[target]:
                issues.append({"url": url, "level": "error",
                               "msg": f"missing return link: {href} ({code}) does not list this page"})
            elif norm(url) not in lang_lookup[target] and code.lower() != "x-default":
                issues.append({"url": url, "level": "warning",
                               "msg": f"{href} links back only through x-default, "
                                      f"with no language-coded entry for this page"})
    return issues

Three decisions are worth explaining.

  1. A page that was not audited is skipped. If page A lists a page the script never fetched, it cannot judge reciprocity, so it stays silent instead of guessing.
  2. A return link that exists only through x-default is a warning, not an error. Google's documentation says links must be reciprocal but does not say whether an x-default entry counts as the link back. A page that points back at you only through x-default has no language-coded entry for you, so I flag it for a human to judge.
  3. Trailing slashes are normalized. https://example.com/de and https://example.com/de/ are treated as the same address when matching, which avoids false return-link errors. If your server treats them as different URLs, that is a separate canonicalization problem.

collect() in the full file fetches the seed page, then each alternate it lists, once each, up to a cap of 30 pages by default. A failed fetch is recorded and the run continues.

Run it 

python hreflang_check.py https://example.com/en/ --max-pages 30

The script exits with status 1 if any error is found, so you can run it in CI after a deploy.

Example output

I ran the audit on three synthetic pages, built to be wrong in a few ways. The English page lists everything. The German page lists only German and French, and the French page uses en-UK with a relative URL. This is the real output of that run, not a live site:

Pages fetched: 3
[error] https://example.com/en/: missing return link: https://example.com/de/ (de) does not list this page
[warning] https://example.com/de/: no x-default entry
[error] https://example.com/fr/: reserved region 'UK' in 'en-UK' is ignored by Google
[error] https://example.com/fr/: 'en-UK' href is not fully qualified: '/uk/'

Notice that the missing return link is reported on the English page, not the German one. The English page claims a German alternate, and the German page does not point back. That is the direction to fix: add the English entry to the German page.

How it was tested

Thirteen offline tests use synthetic HTML strings and a fake fetcher, so they need no network:

pip install pytest
pytest -q test_hreflang_check.py

They cover head-only parsing, mixed-case attributes and multi-token rel, a clean set with no errors, a missing return link, a missing self-reference, a page whose x-default points at itself, a return link that exists only through x-default, code shapes including en_GB and en-UK, relative URLs, duplicate codes, a missing x-default being a warning, trailing-slash matching, fetching each page once with a failing page, and the page cap. All 13 passed.

One test failed on my first run. The cause was my test data, not the code: I had written a page whose x-default pointed back at itself and expected a "does not list itself" error, but that page does appear in its own list. I fixed the test and added one that pins the behavior down.

What this does not do

  • No live testing. I did not run it against a real site, so I cannot say how it behaves with redirects, bot protection, large international sites or slow servers.
  • Shape checks only for codes. As noted above, unknown but well-formed codes pass.
  • HTML method only. HTTP Link headers and sitemap annotations are not read.
  • It does not render JavaScript. If your hreflang tags are injected client-side, the script will not see them. That is also worth knowing, because a crawler reading raw HTML will not see them either.
  • Canonicals are not checked. Hreflang URLs should point to indexable canonical versions. A good next step is to extend the script to compare each alternate's canonical.

Sources

About the author

I am an SEO specialist working on technical SEO, GEO, AEO, entities and international SEO, with 5+ years of experience across 32+ websites, 6 markets and 12+ industries. I write about the parts of SEO that can be checked with a script.

title: SoulKing-AI
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

💀🎸 SoulKing AI — Your Terminal. Your AI. Your Phantom.

What if your Linux terminal had a soul of its own?

Imagine opening your terminal late at night and finding a mysterious digital spirit waiting for you. It can explain Linux commands, analyze potentially dangerous operations, tell creepy stories, and help you explore your system.

Meet SoulKing AI, a haunted, terminal-based Linux assistant that combines local AI, practical Linux utilities, defensive security tools, and a spooky personality.

Built with Python, Rich, SQLite, and the Ollama API, SoulKing transforms the familiar Linux command line into an interactive experience inspired by the Ghost in the Machine theme.

But this ghost isn't completely dependent on the internet. Even when the local AI service is unavailable, SoulKing's built-in utilities and offline story generator can keep working.

Let's explore the machine! 👻

👻 What I Built

SoulKing AI is a terminal-based assistant designed for Kali Linux and other Linux distributions.

I wanted to create something that combines two ideas:

  • A spooky digital companion with a personality.
  • A practical Linux assistant that helps users understand their system and commands.

SoulKing includes three selectable personality modes:

  • 💀 SoulKing Mode: A friendly, humorous, theatrical skeleton-musician spirit.
  • 👻 Ghost Mode: A mysterious personality with spooky responses.
  • 💻 Developer Mode: A technical assistant for Python, Java, Linux, Git, and debugging.

Beyond its personality, SoulKing includes system diagnostics, Linux command assistance, network utilities, command-risk analysis, local SQLite storage, and a ghost story generator.

The project is entirely terminal-based. There is no graphical application window or browser interface.

🖥️ Demo: Inside the Haunted Machine

Here are four screenshots of SoulKing AI running in the terminal.

💀 1. The Haunted Terminal Awakens

The first screen introduces SoulKing's identity through its ASCII banner, terminal prompt, system information, and startup greeting.

It also displays the current AI connection status and confirms that local SQLite memory has been initialized.

In this captured session, Ollama is offline. SoulKing clearly reports the unavailable service instead of pretending that the AI model is running.

That's an important part of the design: the application communicates its actual status to the user.

📜 2. A Command Reference for the Phantom

SoulKing includes a categorized command reference that helps users discover its capabilities.

The available commands cover several areas:

  • General application controls and configuration.
  • System information and diagnostics.
  • Linux command assistance.
  • Local AI model selection and conversations.
  • Network utilities.
  • Defensive security tools.
  • Ghost story generation.

Rather than requiring users to memorize everything, the help command provides a structured overview of the terminal assistant.

🛡️ 3. Command Risk Analyzer and Linux Assistance

This is one of SoulKing's most practical features.

The screenshot demonstrates the command:

risk rm -rf /tmp/example && suggest show listening network ports

SoulKing identifies the recursive deletion operation as high risk and explains why it can permanently remove files. It also suggests a safer alternative.

The command suggestion feature then proposes ss -tuln for displaying listening network ports.

Notice the important detail: the proposed command is never automatically executed.

The screenshot also demonstrates that SoulKing can provide built-in Linux assistance when the Ollama service is disconnected.

Static command analysis is a useful precaution, although it cannot guarantee that every command is safe. Users should always inspect commands and their arguments before running them.

👻 4. Ghost Stories from the Machine

Every haunted terminal needs a storyteller.

This screenshot demonstrates the command:

story short && sysinfo

SoulKing generates a short fictional horror story titled "The Violin in /dev/null".

The story imagines a strange event on a Linux server, where a corrupted core dump and a mysterious melody turn an ordinary system log into a miniature piece of digital horror.

The screenshot identifies the story source as the built-in offline archive because Ollama is disconnected.

After the story, SoulKing displays Linux system information, including the distribution, kernel, architecture, Python version, and working directory.

This is exactly the kind of experience I wanted: a terminal that remains useful while giving users something unexpected.

💻 Code

GitHub Repository: SoulKing-AI

The project is written in Python and released under the MIT License.

The repository contains the source code, terminal screenshots, tests, installation instructions, and configuration documentation.

I built SoulKing to be explored, customized, and extended by other developers.

⚙️ How I Built It

SoulKing uses a terminal-first architecture, keeping the command line as its entire interface.

Technology Stack

  • Python 3.11+: Core application logic and Linux utilities.
  • Rich: Terminal formatting, tables, and an enhanced command-line experience.
  • Ollama: Local model serving through its HTTP API.
  • Llama 3.2: An example open-weight model supported by the project.
  • SQLite: Local storage for conversations, command history, favorites, saved stories, and preferences.
  • TOML: Human-readable application configuration.

The application can also be configured to use another compatible installed model, such as Qwen2.5-Coder.

🧠 Local AI Integration

SoulKing connects to an Ollama service running locally on the machine.

When Ollama is available and a compatible model is installed, users can interact with the assistant through commands such as ask and can generate AI-powered stories.

The application checks the service's availability and reports when it cannot connect.

The screenshots show the offline state, where the built-in story archive and supported Linux assistance features continue to work.

🐧 Linux Utilities

SoulKing includes commands for:

  • Viewing CPU, memory, disk, and uptime information.
  • Listing running processes.
  • Explaining Linux commands and their flags.
  • Suggesting commands for natural-language tasks.
  • Inspecting file permissions.
  • Finding files.
  • Viewing network interfaces and connections.
  • Resolving DNS records and checking host reachability.
  • Analyzing local logs.
  • Checking URL patterns for suspicious characteristics.
  • Identifying installed security and networking tools.
  • Analyzing potentially dangerous command patterns.

The command-risk analyzer and other defensive utilities are designed to help users make more informed decisions when working in a Linux terminal.

📚 Local Memory

SoulKing uses SQLite to store application data, including conversations, messages, command history, favorite commands, saved stories, and preferences.

Users can disable conversation-history saving through the application's configuration.

This local-first approach gives users more control over their saved data.

🔓 Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For me, open innovation is about having the freedom to experiment with AI, customize it, and run it on my own machine rather than making an entire project dependent on a closed API.

SoulKing uses Ollama to run compatible open-weight models locally.

Here is why that matters.

🔒 1. Privacy and Local Control

A Linux assistant may be used to discuss system configurations, examine logs, or troubleshoot a machine.

Running AI locally can help keep those prompts on the user's own computer rather than sending every request to a third-party AI provider.

SoulKing also stores its application history locally by default and provides an option to disable history saving.

📴 2. Offline Resilience

One of the most interesting things about SoulKing is that its core utilities do not all depend on the AI service.

As the screenshots demonstrate, the application can report that Ollama is unreachable while still providing built-in stories, system information, and supported command-analysis functionality.

Once the required software and model have been installed, local AI interactions can also work without an internet connection.

This makes the project useful even when a remote service is unavailable.

🧠 3. Freedom to Experiment

Using a local AI runtime allows developers to experiment with compatible models and customize the assistant's behavior.

SoulKing supports changing the selected model and switching between personality modes.

This flexibility makes it easier to explore different models, prompts, and approaches without redesigning the whole application around one proprietary provider.

💸 4. Fewer Dependencies on Paid APIs

Local inference avoids mandatory per-request fees from a hosted AI API.

It still requires computing resources, memory, electricity, and sufficient hardware for the chosen model, but it gives developers another way to experiment without relying on a paid inference service.

🔓 5. Keeping Projects Under Our Control

A project built entirely around a closed service can be affected by changes in availability, pricing, or access limits.

By using a local runtime and modular components, SoulKing gives developers more control over how their application evolves.

Open innovation is not just about using AI. It's about having the freedom to decide where it runs, how it behaves, and how it can be changed.

🤖 My Agent Session

I used AI-assisted development while building and refining SoulKing's architecture, terminal interactions, and features.

I'm also exploring DevRelay to document the development process for this challenge.

💀 The Spirit of It

"Even without a body, intelligence lives on. Yohohoho!"

The Ghost in the Machine theme made me think about the relationship between computers, memory, and personality.

A terminal is normally a place for commands, logs, and predictable output. SoulKing adds a fictional digital spirit that can tell stories, explain commands, and respond with a little theatrical mischief.

The most interesting part is that the atmosphere does not depend entirely on a live AI connection.

In the screenshots, Ollama is offline, yet SoulKing still tells a story about a mysterious violin in /dev/null.

That small moment captures the idea behind the project: a machine can still have character, even when one of its services goes silent.

The ghost is fictional, but the freedom to experiment with local AI and keep useful software running on our own machines is real.

Maybe the ghost isn't really in the machine.

Maybe it's in the code we choose to keep alive. 👻

🏆 Prize Categories

Thanks for checking out SoulKing AI!

If you enjoy Linux, open-source AI, terminal tools, or spooky software projects, I'd love to hear what you think.

Your terminal. Your AI. Your phantom. 💀🎸

Imagine opening your terminal late at night and finding a mysterious digital spirit waiting for you. It can explain Linux commands, analyze potentially dangerous operations, tell creepy stories, and help you explore your system.

Meet SoulKing AI, a haunted, terminal-based Linux assistant that combines local AI, practical Linux utilities, defensive security tools, and a spooky personality.

Built with Python, Rich, SQLite, and the Ollama API, SoulKing transforms the familiar Linux command line into an interactive experience inspired by the Ghost in the Machine theme.

But this ghost isn't completely dependent on the internet. Even when the local AI service is unavailable, SoulKing's built-in utilities and offline story generator can keep working.

Let's explore the machine! 👻

👻 What I Built

SoulKing AI is a terminal-based assistant designed for Kali Linux and other Linux distributions.

I wanted to create something that combines two ideas:

  • A spooky digital companion with a personality.
  • A practical Linux assistant that helps users understand their system and commands.

SoulKing includes three selectable personality modes:

  • 💀 SoulKing Mode: A friendly, humorous, theatrical skeleton-musician spirit.
  • 👻 Ghost Mode: A mysterious personality with spooky responses.
  • 💻 Developer Mode: A technical assistant for Python, Java, Linux, Git, and debugging.

Beyond its personality, SoulKing includes system diagnostics, Linux command assistance, network utilities, command-risk analysis, local SQLite storage, and a ghost story generator.

The project is entirely terminal-based. There is no graphical application window or browser interface.

🖥️ Demo: Inside the Haunted Machine

Here are four screenshots of SoulKing AI running in the terminal.

💀 1. The Haunted Terminal Awakens

The first screen introduces SoulKing's identity through its ASCII banner, terminal prompt, system information, and startup greeting.

It also displays the current AI connection status and confirms that local SQLite memory has been initialized.

In this captured session, Ollama is offline. SoulKing clearly reports the unavailable service instead of pretending that the AI model is running.

That's an important part of the design: the application communicates its actual status to the user.

📜 2. A Command Reference for the Phantom

SoulKing includes a categorized command reference that helps users discover its capabilities.

The available commands cover several areas:

  • General application controls and configuration.
  • System information and diagnostics.
  • Linux command assistance.
  • Local AI model selection and conversations.
  • Network utilities.
  • Defensive security tools.
  • Ghost story generation.

Rather than requiring users to memorize everything, the help command provides a structured overview of the terminal assistant.

🛡️ 3. Command Risk Analyzer and Linux Assistance

This is one of SoulKing's most practical features.

The screenshot demonstrates the command:

risk rm -rf /tmp/example && suggest show listening network ports

SoulKing identifies the recursive deletion operation as high risk and explains why it can permanently remove files. It also suggests a safer alternative.

The command suggestion feature then proposes ss -tuln for displaying listening network ports.

Notice the important detail: the proposed command is never automatically executed.

The screenshot also demonstrates that SoulKing can provide built-in Linux assistance when the Ollama service is disconnected.

Static command analysis is a useful precaution, although it cannot guarantee that every command is safe. Users should always inspect commands and their arguments before running them.

👻 4. Ghost Stories from the Machine

Every haunted terminal needs a storyteller.

This screenshot demonstrates the command:

story short && sysinfo

SoulKing generates a short fictional horror story titled "The Violin in /dev/null".

The story imagines a strange event on a Linux server, where a corrupted core dump and a mysterious melody turn an ordinary system log into a miniature piece of digital horror.

The screenshot identifies the story source as the built-in offline archive because Ollama is disconnected.

After the story, SoulKing displays Linux system information, including the distribution, kernel, architecture, Python version, and working directory.

This is exactly the kind of experience I wanted: a terminal that remains useful while giving users something unexpected.

💻 Code

GitHub Repository: SoulKing-AI

The project is written in Python and released under the MIT License.

The repository contains the source code, terminal screenshots, tests, installation instructions, and configuration documentation.

I built SoulKing to be explored, customized, and extended by other developers.

⚙️ How I Built It

SoulKing uses a terminal-first architecture, keeping the command line as its entire interface.

Technology Stack

  • Python 3.11+: Core application logic and Linux utilities.
  • Rich: Terminal formatting, tables, and an enhanced command-line experience.
  • Ollama: Local model serving through its HTTP API.
  • Llama 3.2: An example open-weight model supported by the project.
  • SQLite: Local storage for conversations, command history, favorites, saved stories, and preferences.
  • TOML: Human-readable application configuration.

The application can also be configured to use another compatible installed model, such as Qwen2.5-Coder.

🧠 Local AI Integration

SoulKing connects to an Ollama service running locally on the machine.

When Ollama is available and a compatible model is installed, users can interact with the assistant through commands such as ask and can generate AI-powered stories.

The application checks the service's availability and reports when it cannot connect.

The screenshots show the offline state, where the built-in story archive and supported Linux assistance features continue to work.

🐧 Linux Utilities

SoulKing includes commands for:

  • Viewing CPU, memory, disk, and uptime information.
  • Listing running processes.
  • Explaining Linux commands and their flags.
  • Suggesting commands for natural-language tasks.
  • Inspecting file permissions.
  • Finding files.
  • Viewing network interfaces and connections.
  • Resolving DNS records and checking host reachability.
  • Analyzing local logs.
  • Checking URL patterns for suspicious characteristics.
  • Identifying installed security and networking tools.
  • Analyzing potentially dangerous command patterns.

The command-risk analyzer and other defensive utilities are designed to help users make more informed decisions when working in a Linux terminal.

📚 Local Memory

SoulKing uses SQLite to store application data, including conversations, messages, command history, favorite commands, saved stories, and preferences.

Users can disable conversation-history saving through the application's configuration.

This local-first approach gives users more control over their saved data.

🔓 Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For me, open innovation is about having the freedom to experiment with AI, customize it, and run it on my own machine rather than making an entire project dependent on a closed API.

SoulKing uses Ollama to run compatible open-weight models locally.

Here is why that matters.

🔒 1. Privacy and Local Control

A Linux assistant may be used to discuss system configurations, examine logs, or troubleshoot a machine.

Running AI locally can help keep those prompts on the user's own computer rather than sending every request to a third-party AI provider.

SoulKing also stores its application history locally by default and provides an option to disable history saving.

📴 2. Offline Resilience

One of the most interesting things about SoulKing is that its core utilities do not all depend on the AI service.

As the screenshots demonstrate, the application can report that Ollama is unreachable while still providing built-in stories, system information, and supported command-analysis functionality.

Once the required software and model have been installed, local AI interactions can also work without an internet connection.

This makes the project useful even when a remote service is unavailable.

🧠 3. Freedom to Experiment

Using a local AI runtime allows developers to experiment with compatible models and customize the assistant's behavior.

SoulKing supports changing the selected model and switching between personality modes.

This flexibility makes it easier to explore different models, prompts, and approaches without redesigning the whole application around one proprietary provider.

💸 4. Fewer Dependencies on Paid APIs

Local inference avoids mandatory per-request fees from a hosted AI API.

It still requires computing resources, memory, electricity, and sufficient hardware for the chosen model, but it gives developers another way to experiment without relying on a paid inference service.

🔓 5. Keeping Projects Under Our Control

A project built entirely around a closed service can be affected by changes in availability, pricing, or access limits.

By using a local runtime and modular components, SoulKing gives developers more control over how their application evolves.

Open innovation is not just about using AI. It's about having the freedom to decide where it runs, how it behaves, and how it can be changed.

🤖 My Agent Session

I used AI-assisted development while building and refining SoulKing's architecture, terminal interactions, and features.

I'm also exploring DevRelay to document the development process for this challenge.

💀 The Spirit of It

"Even without a body, intelligence lives on. Yohohoho!"

The Ghost in the Machine theme made me think about the relationship between computers, memory, and personality.

A terminal is normally a place for commands, logs, and predictable output. SoulKing adds a fictional digital spirit that can tell stories, explain commands, and respond with a little theatrical mischief.

The most interesting part is that the atmosphere does not depend entirely on a live AI connection.

In the screenshots, Ollama is offline, yet SoulKing still tells a story about a mysterious violin in /dev/null.

That small moment captures the idea behind the project: a machine can still have character, even when one of its services goes silent.

The ghost is fictional, but the freedom to experiment with local AI and keep useful software running on our own machines is real.

Maybe the ghost isn't really in the machine.

Maybe it's in the code we choose to keep alive. 👻

title: Your Polymarket Bot Has Live Prices. That Doesn't Mean It Has the Latest Order Book.
summary:
A trading bot can receive price updates every second and still make decisions using a market state that no longer exists.

That sounds contradictory until you look at how an order book changes.

A bot sees an attractive ask, calculates an edge, and prepares an order. Before that order reaches the exchange, someone cancels the liquidity, another trader takes the offer, or the best available price changes.

The bot's calculation may have been correct when it started. The market it calculated against is gone.

This is one of the problems that separates a bot that merely consumes market data from one that handles live trading conditions properly.

A price is not the same thing as a market state

Imagine your Polymarket bot estimates that a YES share is worth $0.64.

Its market-data handler reports an ask of $0.59, so the strategy identifies a potential five-cent edge.

But three details matter:

  • How recently was that ask observed?
  • How much liquidity was available at that price?
  • Does the price still exist when the order is submitted?

Suppose the $0.59 ask disappears and the next available ask is $0.63.

Your original edge has almost vanished before accounting for fees and other costs.

A system that stores only the latest price can miss the sequence of events that produced this situation. A system that tracks the state of the order book has a better chance of detecting it.

The distinction matters because live market data is a stream of changing observations, not a guarantee that a displayed opportunity will remain executable.

Why WebSocket updates need careful handling

Polymarket's CLOB WebSocket market channel provides events such as order-book snapshots and price changes. Developers can use these events to maintain a local view of the market. See the "Polymarket WebSocket documentation" (https://github.com/Polymarket/agent-skills/blob/main/websocket.md).

The challenge is keeping that local view trustworthy.

A basic implementation might update a variable whenever a new price arrives:

best_ask = incoming_update["best_ask"]

That can be useful for a simple example, but a production system needs more context. Not every event necessarily represents a complete replacement for the order book. Some updates describe changes to particular prices or assets.

If the bot treats every message as a full snapshot, it can lose information. If it applies updates incorrectly, its local book can diverge from the exchange's current state.

The result is a strategy making decisions from data that looks valid but is incomplete.

Build a local book, not just a price variable

A more robust architecture separates market-data ingestion from strategy execution.

The data layer receives events and updates the local order book. The strategy reads a consistent view of that book, evaluates the opportunity, and passes a proposed order to an execution layer.

That execution layer performs its own checks before submission.

A simplified flow looks like this:

WebSocket events
|
v
Event validation
|
v
Local order-book state
|
v
Strategy evaluation
|
v
Pre-trade validation
|
v
Order submission
|
v
Fill and order-status tracking

Each stage has a separate responsibility.

The data layer should understand the event types it receives. The strategy should calculate its edge using the appropriate side of the book. The execution layer should reject orders that no longer satisfy the strategy's price, size, or risk constraints.

This separation also makes debugging easier. If a trade performs badly, you can investigate whether the problem came from the signal, the book state, or execution.

What should happen after a disconnect?

Consider a more dangerous situation.

Your bot loses its WebSocket connection for several seconds. During that period, prices move and orders are cancelled. The connection reconnects, and new messages begin arriving.

Should the bot immediately resume trading?

Not necessarily.

The system first needs to establish whether its local market state is trustworthy. Depending on the documented protocol and the events received, that may require obtaining a fresh book snapshot and rebuilding local state before allowing new decisions.

A conservative recovery procedure is:

  1. Mark the affected market data as unavailable or untrusted.
  2. Stop generating new orders that depend on that state.
  3. Reconnect and restore the local book using the supported snapshot-and-update process.
  4. Validate the reconstructed state before enabling the strategy again.
  5. Reconcile outstanding orders and fills separately from market-data recovery.

The last point is easy to overlook. Restoring the order book does not tell you whether an order submitted before the disconnect was accepted, partially filled, or still resting. Account and order state need their own reconciliation process.

A reconnect is not proof that everything is synchronized.

Add a pre-trade freshness check

Even a correctly maintained local book can become outdated between the strategy's calculation and order submission.

Your bot should therefore define what it considers an acceptable data state before placing an order.

For example, a pre-trade validator might check:

  • Whether the market-data connection is healthy.
  • Whether the local book has been initialized and remains valid.
  • Whether the latest relevant update falls within the strategy's configured freshness limit.
  • Whether the intended size is supported by available liquidity.
  • Whether the executable price still leaves enough expected edge after estimated costs.

The freshness limit should depend on the strategy. A bot reacting to rapid price changes may require stricter limits than one trading infrequently.

Also, do not assume that a recent message automatically proves that the entire book is synchronized. Freshness and consistency are related, but they are not interchangeable.

Test the failures, not just the happy path

A bot that works while the network is stable has passed only one part of its engineering test.

Build tests that simulate:

  • A price changing immediately before order submission.
  • Liquidity disappearing at the intended entry price.
  • A disconnect followed by reconnection.
  • Duplicate or unexpected events.
  • A partially filled order during a market-data interruption.
  • A book that cannot be confidently reconstructed.

For each scenario, define the expected behavior before running the test. Should the bot reject the trade, pause the market, rebuild state, or reconcile an outstanding order?

That turns resilience from a vague objective into something measurable.

You can start with recorded market-data events and simulated order responses before introducing real capital. A deterministic replay also makes it easier to reproduce a bug that occurred during a live session.

The real objective is trustworthy decisions

Real-time data is valuable only when the system understands what that data represents and when it is safe to act on it.

For Polymarket bot developers, this means treating the order book as state that must be maintained and validated, not as a number that can simply be overwritten whenever a message arrives.

The strongest implementation is not necessarily the one that reacts to every update fastest. It is the one that knows when its view of the market is reliable, when an opportunity has disappeared, and when it should refuse to trade.

That discipline will not guarantee profitable trades. It will, however, help prevent avoidable execution mistakes from being mistaken for strategy failures.

title: Import Word Table Data into Excel Using Python
summary:
Tables in Word documents often contain structured data, but Excel is better suited for analyzing, filtering, and charting that data. When a document contains multiple tables, copying and pasting them manually can be time-consuming and may introduce errors during conversion.

This article explains how to use Spire.Doc for Python and Spire.XLS for Python to import each table from a Word document into a separate Excel worksheet. It also describes what the solution can handle and where its limitations lie.

Install the Required Libraries

Before you begin, install two libraries: Spire.Doc reads and parses the table structure in Word documents, while Spire.XLS creates and writes Excel files. Run the following commands:

pip install Spire.Doc
pip install Spire.XLS

Spire products also offer free editions, such as spire.doc.free and spire.xls.free, which you can install with pip install spire.doc.free spire.xls.free. The free editions have certain limitations. For example, Free Spire.Doc supports up to 500 paragraphs and 25 tables per document. The free editions may be sufficient for smaller documents, while larger documents or those containing more tables require the full versions.

Both libraries support Windows, Linux, and macOS, and neither requires Microsoft Office or Word to be installed.

How the Conversion Works

The conversion process can be divided into two stages:

Extraction: Load the Word document and iterate through each section, then through each table in that section. For every cell, read and combine the text from all its paragraphs to retain content that spans multiple paragraphs.

Writing: Create a new Excel workbook and a separate worksheet for each Word table. Write the extracted text to the corresponding cells in row and column order, automatically adjust the column widths, and save the file.

Complete Code Example

The following code implements this process. It is written for the full versions of the Spire libraries. If you use the free editions, adjust the import statements to from spire.doc import * and from spire.xls import *, respectively.

from spire.doc import *
from spire.xls import *

# Load the Word document
doc = Document()
doc.LoadFromFile('input.docx')

# Create an Excel workbook and remove the default worksheets
wb = Workbook()
wb.Worksheets.Clear()

# Iterate through all sections in the document
for i in range(doc.Sections.Count):
    section = doc.Sections.get_Item(i)

    # Iterate through all tables in the section
    for j in range(section.Tables.Count):
        table = section.Tables.get_Item(j)

        # Create a worksheet for each table, using the section and table numbers
        ws = wb.Worksheets.Add(f'Table_{i+1}_{j+1}')

        # Write data one row and one cell at a time
        for row in range(table.Rows.Count):
            tableRow = table.Rows.get_Item(row)

            for cell in range(tableRow.Cells.Count):
                tableCell = tableRow.Cells.get_Item(cell)

                # Combine the text of all paragraphs in the cell
                cellText = ''
                for paragraph in range(tableCell.Paragraphs.Count):
                    paragraph = tableCell.Paragraphs.get_Item(paragraph)

title: 'wise' Is a Printing Company Founded in 1969. The 404s Were the Good Outcome
summary:
I run a visa agency in Bali, and the other half of my week goes into Apify Actors. One of them reads public LinkedIn company pages and returns firmographics as a flat row: website, industry, size band, employees on LinkedIn, followers, headquarters with street address, company type, founded year, specialties, every office, similar pages, affiliated pages.

The input is a LinkedIn company URL. The problem is that nobody's lead list contains LinkedIn company URLs. Lead lists contain brand names — a conference attendee sheet, a column pasted out of a CRM, the output of some other scraper. So the first thing everyone does, including me, is build the URL by hand:

slug = brand.lower().replace(" ", "")
url  = f"https://www.linkedin.com/company/{slug}"

On 27 October 2026 I ran that guess against 38 well-known brands and looked at what came back. Here is the summary before the details, because the shape of it is the point:

38 guessed slugs
  32  the company I meant
   2  HTTP 404 — free, not charged
   4  a different company — complete row, charged, no warning

The two 404s were Tesla and Plaid. They cost nothing, they arrive as an error row with a reason, and they are impossible to miss. The four that worked are the expensive ones.

The four

Guessed slug name industry HQ employeesOnLinkedIn followers website
wise Wise Printing Services Alpharetta, GA 265 1,708 wbf.com
uber Uber Agency Advertising Services Leeds 1,018 6,023 uberagency.com
square SQUARE Advertising Services Oslo 55 391 square.co
gitlab Domify Information Technology & Services Nõmme, Harjumaa 3 3,172 domify.io

linkedin.com/company/wise is Wise, a trade printer in Georgia making business forms, prescription pads and jumbo label rolls since 1969. Five plants, 265 people on LinkedIn, and a completely legitimate row:

{
  "name": "Wise",
  "linkedinUrl": "https://www.linkedin.com/company/wise",
  "website": "http://www.wbf.com",
  "tagline": "Forms l Labels l Digital",
  "industry": "Printing Services",
  "companySize": "201-500 employees",
  "employeesOnLinkedIn": 265,
  "followers": 1708,
  "headquarters": "Alpharetta, GA",
  "streetAddress": "555 McFarland 400 Dr.",
  "companyType": "Privately Held",
  "founded": 1969,
  "specialties": ["Business Forms & Checks", "Unit Sets", "Prescription Pads", "Jumbo Rolls"]
}

The fintech lives at wiseaccount (and transferwise, which resolves to the same page): 11,852 employees, 715,775 followers, London, founded 2011.

Nothing in that row is wrong. Every field is populated, the address is real, the specialties are real. If it lands in a CRM next to "Wise — fintech, London", the only thing that will flag it is a human reading the tagline.

Name matching does not save you

The obvious defence is to compare the name the page returned against the brand you asked for. Normalise both to lowercase alphanumerics and check equality:

  • gitlab → domify — caught.
  • uber → uberagency — caught.
  • wise → wise — not caught.
  • square → square — not caught.

Two of four. And the two it misses are the two that matter most, because an exact name collision is precisely the case where a brand did not get its own slug. That is not a coincidence — the companies that lost the race for /company/wise lost it to another company called Wise.

Guessing harder makes it worse, not better. My second round of guesses:

plaid           → 404                (free)
plaid-inc       → PLAID, Inc.        324 employees, plaid.co.jp — a Japanese software company
plaid-technologies → 404             (free)

square          → SQUARE             55 employees, Oslo ad agency
square-inc      → SQUARE Inc.        2 employees, square-shop.ocnk.net — Japanese furniture
squareup        → 404                (free)
block           → Block              287 employees, no website at all
joinsquare      → Square             6,252 employees, squareup.com — the payments company

Four plausible guesses for Square's page. One right. Every wrong one carried "Square" or "Block" in the name and came back fully populated.

What actually separates them

Three signals in the row work, and none of them is the name.

The website domain. All four wrong rows published a website, and all four domains were visibly not the brand's: wbf.com, uberagency.com, square.co, domify.io. If your source list has a domain in it — and lead lists usually do — comparing registrable domains catches 4 of 4. This is the check to build first.

Follower count. The four wrong rows had 391, 1,708, 3,172 and 6,023 followers. The lowest follower count among the 32 correct pages was Intercom at 191,393. A 31× gap with nothing in between. For a list of companies you have heard of, a floor of 50,000 followers would have flagged all four and nothing else. Worth knowing the limit of this one: it only works because recognisable brand implies large page. On a list of 20-person manufacturers it is useless.

similarCompanies — the part I did not expect. LinkedIn's own "similar pages" rail on the wrong page points at the right one in three of the four cases:

wise    (printer)     → Revolut, Wise /company/wiseaccount, Monzo, Stripe, Adyen, N26, Klarna, PayPal
uber    (ad agency)   → Uber /company/uber-com, Airbnb, Amazon, Salesforce, Microsoft, Adobe
gitlab  (Domify)      → Automattic, Zapier, Toptal, GitLab /company/gitlab-com, Canonical
square  (Oslo agency) → Dropbox, Toast, PayPal, Elastic, Lightspeed Commerce, Shopify

LinkedIn's recommender has clearly been trained on what people searching that page actually wanted. So the recovery is automatable: when the domain check fails, scan similarCompanies for a name that matches your brand, take its linkedinUrl, and re-run that one slug. Three of my four repaired themselves that way. The fourth — Square — did not get a direct hit, but its rail is unmistakably the payments neighbourhood, which is enough to tell a human they are on the wrong page.

Running it 

{
  "companies": ["wiseaccount", "uber-com", "gitlab-com", "joinsquare"],
  "includePosts": false
}

Slugs and full URLs are both accepted. From Python, with the domain check attached:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("")
targets = {"wiseaccount": "wise.com", "uber-com": "uber.com"}

run = client.actor("lergassy/linkedin-company-scraper").call(run_input={
    "companies": list(targets),
    "includePosts": False,
})

for row in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if row.get("type") != "company":
        continue
    host = (row.get("website") or "").split("//")[-1].split("/")[0].removeprefix("www.")
    ok = host.endswith(targets[row["slug"]])
    print(row["slug"], row["name"], row["employeesOnLinkedIn"], host, "OK" if ok else "MISMATCH")

Full run details and field list are on the LinkedIn Company Scraper page. Error rows and 404s are not billed, which is why the loud failures are also the free ones.

A second disagreement, while I had the data

Two fields in every row claim to describe headcount, and they come from different places in the page. companySize is the band the company picked in its own page settings, parsed out of the About dl. employeesOnLinkedIn is LinkedIn's count of members who list that company as their employer, read out of the page's JSON-LD.

Across the 36 rows that landed on the company I meant — the 32 good guesses, plus the repaired slugs and the two I knew by hand — 26 had a closed band (not the open-ended 10,001+). Of those 26, 15 reported more employees on LinkedIn than their own band's ceiling allows, and zero reported fewer than the floor:

Airbnb      5,001-10,000 employees   →  73,151   ×7.3
Notion        501-1,000 employees    →   7,211   ×7.2
Anthropic     501-1,000 employees    →   6,244   ×6.2
Canva       1,001-5,000 employees    →  20,019   ×4.0
Duolingo      501-1,000 employees    →   3,274   ×3.3
OpenAI      1,001-5,000 employees    →  11,490   ×2.3
Datadog     1,001-5,000 employees    →  10,333   ×2.1

The error is one-directional, which tells you it is not noise. Members keep listing an employer after they leave, contractors and franchisees list the brand they work under, and nobody goes back to update the band after a hiring year. Neither number is a headcount. One is a declaration the company made once, the other is a tally of profiles.

Practical consequence: "51–200 employees in SaaS" filtered on companySizeMin/companySizeMax and the same filter on employeesOnLinkedIn return different lists, and the second one skews large. Pick one, write down which, and do not mix them across refreshes of the same list.

When this is the wrong tool

It reads what a logged-out visitor sees, so there is no employee list — the count and the band, never the people. Follower counts on similar pages, the verified badge and the number of open roles are also logged-in-only, so they are not in the row. And it will not find a page from a name: it resolves URLs, it does not search. That gap is the subject of this post, and the honest answer is that brand → slug is a separate job with its own failure mode, not a flag you switch on.

One last detail, noticed only because Wise's page answers to two slugs and I read both: followers came back 715,775 on one read and 715,776 on the next. Identical page, identical everything else. If you diff weekly snapshots, that is the floor of your noise.

title: Why StareBrain’s AI Backend Writes Nothing to a Database: A Stateless Agent Architecture
summary:
Introduction

Most backend services own state. They write to a database, track sessions, remember where you are in a flow.

StareBrain’s backend does none of that. Every request to /next-step is self-contained. The backend reads what the client sends, decides the next action, and returns it. Nothing is written. Nothing is stored. The session ends when the response leaves.

This is a deliberate architectural choice — and it has real consequences for how the agent handles plans, step history, and recovery.

The Request and Response

The full schema for a single agent step:

`class AgentStepRequest(BaseModel):
    task: str
    screen_description: str
    current_package: Optional[str] = None
    steps_so_far: list[str] = []
    step_count: int
    known_facts: str = ""
    plan: list[str] = []
    current_subgoal: int = 0
    screenshot_b64: Optional[str] = None
    capabilities: list[str] = []

class AgentStepResponse(BaseModel):
    reasoning: Optional[str] = None
    action: str
    target_index: Optional[int] = None
    text_to_type: Optional[str] = None
    app_name: Optional[str] = None
    setting_name: Optional[str] = None
    status_text: str
    final_answer: Optional[str] = None
    remember: Optional[RememberFact] = None
    plan: Optional[list[str]] = None
    advance_subgoal: bool = False
    replan: Optional[list[str]] = None
    requires_confirmation: bool = False

title: Blur faces in video with MediaPipe and FFmpeg (without the flicker)
summary:
📦 Code: github.com/USER/video-redact (replace before publishing)

TL;DR

We'll turn per-frame face detections into padded, time-held blur regions and render them with a single FFmpeg filter graph. You get: no flicker on missed frames, audio copied untouched, one re-encode. Python 3.10+, mediapipe 0.10.x, FFmpeg 6+.

🎯 The problem

A face detector gives you one box per face per frame. Blur exactly those boxes and the blur flickers whenever the detector misses a frame, which is when someone turns their head. In a redaction pipeline, the flicker frame is the leak.

So we do three things to the raw detections:

  1. Pad each box so the hairline and jaw are covered.
  2. Hold each detection for N frames so a missed frame is bridged.
  3. Merge overlapping boxes in space and time into one wider region.

Then we render with FFmpeg: crop, blur, overlay, enabled only during each region's time window.

⚠️ Note: The detection step below was not run on real faces by me (no face footage or model download in my test environment). The padding, hold, merge and FFmpeg rendering steps were tested on a synthetic clip with hand-written boxes. Measure recall on your own footage before trusting any of it.

1. Set up 🛠️ 

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install mediapipe opencv-python
# download a face detector model (BlazeFace short range) per the MediaPipe docs
# and save it as blaze_face_short_range.tflite
ffmpeg -version | head -1

2. Detect faces, frame by frame

This follows the MediaPipe Tasks API in video mode. Check the current docs for exact option names in your version.

# detect.py
import json, sys
import cv2
import mediapipe as mp
from mediapipe.tasks import python as mp_python
from mediapipe.tasks.python import vision

path, model = sys.argv[1], "blaze_face_short_range.tflite"
opts = vision.FaceDetectorOptions(
    base_options=mp_python.BaseOptions(model_asset_path=model),
    running_mode=vision.RunningMode.VIDEO,
    min_detection_confidence=0.3,   # low on purpose: for redaction, recall beats precision
)
cap = cv2.VideoCapture(path)
fps = cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)
w, h = int(cap.get(3)), int(cap.get(4))
dets, i = {}, 0
with vision.FaceDetector.create_from_options(opts) as det:
    while True:
        ok, frame = cap.read()
        if not ok:
            break
        img = mp.Image(image_format=mp.ImageFormat.SRGB,
                       data=cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))
        res = det.detect_for_video(img, int(i * 1000 / fps))
        boxes = [[b.bounding_box.origin_x, b.bounding_box.origin_y,
                  b.bounding_box.width, b.bounding_box.height]
                 for b in res.detections]
        if boxes:
            dets[i] = boxes
        i += 1
json.dump(dets, open("boxes.json", "w"))
print(f"fps={fps} size={w}x{h} frames_with_faces={len(dets)}/{i}")

Note the deliberately low confidence threshold. A false positive costs you a blurred poster. A false negative costs you a published face.

3. Pad, hold, merge ✅

This is the tested part. boxes.json maps frame index to a list of [x, y, w, h].

# redact.py
import json, sys

def hold_and_pad(dets, fps, w, h, pad=0.35, hold_frames=15):
    out = []
    for f, boxes in sorted(dets.items(), key=lambda kv: int(kv[0])):
        f = int(f)
        for x, y, bw, bh in boxes:
            px, py = bw * pad, bh * pad
            x0, y0 = max(0, int(x - px)), max(0, int(y - py))
            x1, y1 = min(w, int(x + bw + px)), min(h, int(y + bh + py))
            # each detection covers [f, f + hold_frames): bridges missed frames
            out.append((f / fps, (f + hold_frames) / fps, x0, y0, x1 - x0, y1 - y0))
    return out

def _overlap(a, b):
    ax0, ay0, ax1, ay1 = a[2], a[3], a[2] + a[4], a[3] + a[5]
    bx0, by0, bx1, by1 = b[2], b[3], b[2] + b[4], b[3] + b[5]
    return ax0 < bx1 and bx0 < ax1 and ay0 < by1 and by0 < ay1

def merge(regions):
    """Union boxes that overlap in space AND in time into one wider region."""
    merged = []
    for r in sorted(regions, key=lambda r: r[0]):
        for i, m in enumerate(merged):
            if r[0] <= m[1] and _overlap(m, r):
                x0, y0 = min(m[2], r[2]), min(m[3], r[3])
                x1 = max(m[2] + m[4], r[2] + r[4]); y1 = max(m[3] + m[5], r[3] + r[5])
                merged[i] = (min(m[0], r[0]), max(m[1], r[1]), x0, y0, x1 - x0, y1 - y0)
                break
        else:
            merged.append(r)
    return merged

def to_filter(regions):
    if not regions:
        return "null", "[0:v]"
    parts, cur = [], "[0:v]"
    for i, (t0, t1, x, y, bw, bh) in enumerate(regions):
        nxt = f"[v{i}]"
        en = f"between(t,{t0:.3f},{t1:.3f})"
        parts.append(f"{cur}split[a{i}][b{i}];"
                     f"[b{i}]crop={bw}:{bh}:{x}:{y},boxblur=luma_radius=min(w\\,h)/4:luma_power=3[bl{i}];"
                     f"[a{i}][bl{i}]overlay={x}:{y}:enable='{en}'{nxt}")
        cur = nxt
    return ";".join(parts), cur

if __name__ == "__main__":
    dets = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
    fps, w, h = float(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3]), int(sys.argv[4])
    g, last = to_filter(merge(hold_and_pad(dets, fps, w, h)))
    print(g)
    print(last, file=sys.stderr)

Try it with a hand-written file (a face drifting over three frames with one missed, then a second face later):

{"10": [[200,100,80,80]], "11": [[204,100,80,80]], "13": [[212,102,80,80]], "60": [[400,200,60,60]]}

python3 redact.py boxes.json 30 640 360 > graph.txt 2> last.txt
cat graph.txt

[0:v]split[a0][b0];[b0]crop=148:138:172:72,boxblur=luma_radius=min(w\,h)/4:luma_power=3[bl0];[a0][bl0]overlay=172:72:enable='between(t,0.333,0.933)'[v0];[v0]split[a1][b1];[b1]crop=102:102:379:179,boxblur=luma_radius=min(w\,h)/4:luma_power=3[bl1];[a1][bl1]overlay=379:179:enable='between(t,2.000,2.500)'[v1]

Four detections became two regions: frames 10 to 13 merged into one wider box (the missed frame 12 is covered), and the later face got its own window.

4. Render with FFmpeg 🎬 

ffmpeg -hide_banner -y -i in.mp4 \
  -filter_complex "$(cat graph.txt)" \
  -map "$(cat last.txt)" -map 0:a \
  -c:v libx264 -crf 23 -c:a copy out.mp4

ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_name,nb_frames -of csv out.mp4

stream,h264,120
stream,aac,174

All 120 video frames survive, and the audio is a stream copy, not re-encoded.

💡 Tip: If your source can have no audio, use -map 0:a? so the missing stream isn't an error.

⚠️ Note: One split/overlay pair per region is fine for short clips. For long footage with hundreds of regions, render in chunks and concatenate, or you'll hit slow filter graph setup.

5. Quality control (the real work) 🔍

No metric tells you a face leaked. So:

  • Sample frames from every output, weighted toward the second after each hold ends.
  • Review scene cuts and entrances/exits.
  • Measure recall yourself: take 30 seconds of your worst footage and count frames with a visible face and no box.

Blurring is also not anonymization. Voices, name badges, license plates and the room itself can identify people, and there may be legal obligations depending on where you operate. Ask counsel.

What's next

  • Add a tracker (OpenCV trackers or IoU matching) to bridge longer misses than a half-second hold.
  • Swap boxblur for pixelize if your reviewers prefer an obviously redacted look.
  • Run detection every Nth frame to cut compute, then raise hold_frames to match.

If you tune the pad and hold values on real footage, share what worked in the comments. #python #ffmpeg #video #tutorial

title: FFmpeg 9.0 upgrade check: a 60-line harness that diffs your recipes across two builds
summary:
📦 Code: github.com/USER/ffmpeg-upgrade-check (replace before publishing)

TL;DR

FFmpeg 9.0 "Lei" (released 2026-08-04) bumped every core library and removed some old support. Exit code 0 does not mean "same output". We'll build a ~60 line Python script that runs your real command lines with the old and new ffmpeg, then diffs ffprobe fields and SSIM. Python 3.10+, any ffmpeg.

🎯 What we're building

A script that takes two ffmpeg binaries, one source clip, and a JSON file of your recipes, and prints OK, DIFF, or FAIL for each one. Think of it as a snapshot test where the snapshot is "whatever the old build did".

What changed in 9.0, per the release coverage I read (news write-ups, not the changelog itself, so skim the official notes for your own recipes):

Area Change
Libraries Every core library got a major bump; libavcodec and libavformat are in the 63 series
Removed Standalone CELT decoding and Ogg/CELT parsing (Opus is not affected)
Removed NVIDIA Video Codec SDK versions before 11.1, plus previously deprecated NVENC options
Added ONNX Runtime DNN backend on GPU, v360_vulkan, transpose_cuda, native animated WebP decode, LCEVC track muxing in MP4

1. Pick the recipes that matter 🛠️

title: Add speaker labels to video captions with WhisperX and WebVTT voice spans
summary:
TL;DR

We'll turn a two-person video into a WebVTT caption file where each cue says who is speaking. Pipeline: ffmpeg extracts audio, whisperx --diarize transcribes and labels speakers, a small Python script groups words into cues.

Plain speech-to-text gives you a wall of words. For interviews, podcasts and meetings, readers need to know who said what. We'll use WhisperX (Whisper with voice activity detection, forced alignment and pyannote-based diarization) and the standard WebVTT voice span so any player can show the names. #python #video

You'll need python 3.10+, ffmpeg, a Hugging Face account, and ideally a CUDA GPU. CPU works with --compute_type int8 --device cpu, just slower.

1. 🔑 Get access to the diarization model

WhisperX's diarization uses pyannote's speaker-diarization-community-1 pipeline, which is gated on Hugging Face:

  1. Create a read token at hf.co/settings/tokens.
  2. Open the pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1 model page and accept the user conditions. 
export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx   # never commit this

⚠️ Note: if you skip the user-conditions step, the pipeline fails to load with an authorization error even with a valid token. Accept the conditions first.

2. 🎧 Extract audio from the video 

# extract_audio.sh
ffmpeg -y -i interview.mp4 -vn -ac 1 -ar 16000 audio.wav

Mono, 16 kHz is what speech models work with internally, and a WAV file avoids decoder surprises.

3. 🗣️ Transcribe and diarize 

pip install whisperx
whisperx audio.wav --model large-v2 --diarize --hf_token "$HF_TOKEN" \
  --output_format json --output_dir out

On CPU:

whisperx audio.wav --model large-v2 --diarize --hf_token "$HF_TOKEN" \
  --compute_type int8 --device cpu --output_format json --output_dir out

The README lists the CPU flags and the diarize flag. WhisperX does four things in order: voice activity detection, Whisper transcription, wav2vec2 forced alignment (word-level timestamps), then pyannote diarization with speakers assigned to words.

💡 Tip: WhisperX's README claims 70x realtime for large-v2 batched transcription. That's their best case. Time it on your own hardware before planning capacity.

4. 🔍 Look at the JSON

Each segment has a speaker, and each aligned word carries one too (shortened example):

{
  "segments": [
    {
      "start": 0.5, "end": 4.2,
      "text": "Welcome back to the show.",
      "speaker": "SPEAKER_00",
      "words": [
        {"word": "Welcome", "start": 0.5, "end": 1.0, "speaker": "SPEAKER_00"},
        {"word": "42", "speaker": "SPEAKER_01"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Notice the last word: numbers and symbols often come back with no start/end. Our converter has to skip those or it will crash.

⚠️ Note: the exact JSON fields can shift between WhisperX versions. Open one real output file and confirm words[].speaker exists before trusting the script below.

5. 🧩 Group words into WebVTT cues

The rules:

  • a new cue starts when the speaker changes,
  • or after a pause longer than 1.5 s,
  • or when a cue would run longer than 7 s (so captions stay readable). 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Convert WhisperX JSON (with --diarize) into a WebVTT file using  voice spans."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys

MAX_CUE_SECONDS = 7.0   # split long monologues so captions stay readable
GAP_SECONDS = 1.5       # a pause this long starts a new cue even for the same speaker


def ts(seconds: float) -> str:
    ms = round(seconds * 1000)
    h, ms = divmod(ms, 3_600_000)
    m, ms = divmod(ms, 60_000)
    s, ms = divmod(ms, 1000)
    return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}.{ms:03d}"


def words_with_speakers(data: dict) -> list[dict]:
    out = []
    last_speaker = "UNKNOWN"
    for seg in data["segments"]:
        for w in seg.get("words", []):
            if "start" not in w:          # numbers and symbols often get no timestamp
                continue
            last_speaker = w.get("speaker", seg.get("speaker", last_speaker))
            out.append({"word": w["word"], "start": w["start"], "end": w["end"], "speaker": last_speaker})
    return out


def build_cues(words: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    cues, cur = [], None
    for w in words:
        new = (
            cur is None
            or w["speaker"] != cur["speaker"]
            or w["start"] - cur["end"] > GAP_SECONDS
            or w["end"] - cur["start"] > MAX_CUE_SECONDS
        )
        if new:
            cur = {"speaker": w["speaker"], "start": w["start"], "end": w["end"], "text": [w["word"]]}
            cues.append(cur)
        else:
            cur["text"].append(w["word"])
            cur["end"] = w["end"]
    return cues


def to_vtt(cues: list[dict], names: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    lines = ["WEBVTT", ""]
    for i, c in enumerate(cues, 1):
        name = names.get(c["speaker"], c["speaker"])
        lines += [str(i), f"{ts(c['start'])} --> {ts(c['end'])}", f"{name}>{' '.join(c['text'])}", ""]
    return "\n".join(lines)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
    names = json.loads(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else {}
    print(to_vtt(build_cues(words_with_speakers(data)), names))

Run it, mapping the generic labels to names you know:

python3 diar_to_vtt.py out/audio.json '{"SPEAKER_00":"Host","SPEAKER_01":"Guest"}' > captions.vtt

On a small hand-written sample in the same shape as WhisperX output, the result is:

WEBVTT

1
00:00:00.500 --> 00:00:02.100
Welcome back to the show.

2
00:00:02.600 --> 00:00:04.100
Thanks for having me.

The syntax is the WebVTT voice span from the W3C spec. The closing can be omitted when the span covers the whole cue, which is the case here.

6. ▶️ Attach it to a player 


 controls src="interview.mp4">
   kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" src="captions.vtt" default />

HLS players take the same file as a subtitles rendition if you package it. Style the speaker with the ::cue(v[voice="Host"]) selector.

/* captions.css */
video::cue(v[voice="Host"]) { color: #ffd166; }
video::cue(v[voice="Guest"]) { color: #8ecae6; }

7. 🚧 Limits to know before shipping

Limit What happens What to do
Generic labels Output says SPEAKER_00, not a name Map by hand, from invite metadata, or a speaker-ID step
Per-file labels SPEAKER_00 in one file is not SPEAKER_00 in another Carry identity yourself across recordings
Overlapping speech One word gets one speaker Review a sample of crosstalk-heavy content
Model accuracy pyannote reports 11.2 DER on VoxConverse for community-1 (project's own benchmark) Score on your own labelled sample

What's next

  • Score your own accuracy: hand-label ten minutes of your content and compute diarization error rate against it.
  • Index the speaker field so search can answer "what did the guest say about X".
  • If your content has fixed hosts, look at speaker-embedding matching to name them automatically.

Wrapping up: three commands and one small script give you captions that identify speakers, in a format every player already understands.

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys

MAX_CUE_SECONDS = 7.0   # split long monologues so captions stay readable
GAP_SECONDS = 1.5       # a pause this long starts a new cue even for the same speaker


def ts(seconds: float) -> str:
    ms = round(seconds * 1000)
    h, ms = divmod(ms, 3_600_000)
    m, ms = divmod(ms, 60_000)
    s, ms = divmod(ms, 1000)
    return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}.{ms:03d}"


def words_with_speakers(data: dict) -> list[dict]:
    out = []
    last_speaker = "UNKNOWN"
    for seg in data["segments"]:
        for w in seg.get("words", []):
            if "start" not in w:          # numbers and symbols often get no timestamp
                continue
            last_speaker = w.get("speaker", seg.get("speaker", last_speaker))
            out.append({"word": w["word"], "start": w["start"], "end": w["end"], "speaker": last_speaker})
    return out


def build_cues(words: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    cues, cur = [], None
    for w in words:
        new = (
            cur is None
            or w["speaker"] != cur["speaker"]
            or w["start"] - cur["end"] > GAP_SECONDS
            or w["end"] - cur["start"] > MAX_CUE_SECONDS
        )
        if new:
            cur = {"speaker": w["speaker"], "start": w["start"], "end": w["end"], "text": [w["word"]]}
            cues.append(cur)
        else:
            cur["text"].append(w["word"])
            cur["end"] = w["end"]
    return cues


def to_vtt(cues: list[dict], names: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    lines = ["WEBVTT", ""]
    for i, c in enumerate(cues, 1):
        name = names.get(c["speaker"], c["speaker"])
        lines += [str(i), f"{ts(c['start'])} --> {ts(c['end'])}", f"{name}>{' '.join(c['text'])}", ""]
    return "\n".join(lines)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
    names = json.loads(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else {}
    print(to_vtt(build_cues(words_with_speakers(data)), names))

Run it, mapping the generic labels to names you know:

On a small hand-written sample in the same shape as WhisperX output, the result is:

WEBVTT

1
00:00:00.500 --> 00:00:02.100
Welcome back to the show.

2
00:00:02.600 --> 00:00:04.100
Thanks for having me.

The syntax is the WebVTT voice span from the W3C spec. The closing can be omitted when the span covers the whole cue, which is the case here.

6. ▶️ Attach it to a player 


 controls src="interview.mp4">
   kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" src="captions.vtt" default />

HLS players take the same file as a subtitles rendition if you package it. Style the speaker with the ::cue(v[voice="Host"]) selector.

/* captions.css */
video::cue(v[voice="Host"]) { color: #ffd166; }
video::cue(v[voice="Guest"]) { color: #8ecae6; }

7. 🚧 Limits to know before shipping

Limit What happens What to do
Generic labels Output says SPEAKER_00, not a name Map by hand, from invite metadata, or a speaker-ID step
Per-file labels SPEAKER_00 in one file is not SPEAKER_00 in another Carry identity yourself across recordings
Overlapping speech One word gets one speaker Review a sample of crosstalk-heavy content

What's next

  • Score your own accuracy: hand-label ten minutes of your content and compute diarization error rate against it.
  • Index the speaker field so search can answer "what did the guest say about X".
  • If your content has fixed hosts, look at speaker-embedding matching to name them automatically.
